Struc- tural integration degrades under progressive dis- closure on both platforms, while semantic com- ponent faithfulness degrades substantially on Claude Code and remains approximately sta- ble on Codex. These conclusions persist under stricter exposure filters and a targeted human correction of judge false-absence errors. As a mitigation case study, ProjectGuard main- tains external semantic and structural project state and recovers 90% of Claude Code’s mea- sured faithfulness gap. Code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/lunaryan/drift-benchmark.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Macro: Enhancing Multilingual Counterfactual Explanations through Alignment-as-Preference Optimization
abstract: Self-generated counterfactual explanations (SCEs) are minimally modified inputs minimality generated by large language models (LLMs) that flip their own predictions validity, offering a causally grounded approach to unraveling black-box LLM behavior. Yet extending them beyond English remains challenging: existing methods struggle to produce valid SCEs in non-dominant languages, and a persistent trade-off between validity and minimality undermines explanation quality. We introduce Macro, a preference alignment framework that applies Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to multilingual SCE generation, using a composite scoring function to construct preference pairs that effectively translate the trade-off into measurable preference signals. Experiments across four LLMs and seven typologically diverse languages show that Macro improves validity by 12.55% on average over the chain-of-thought baseline without degrading minimality, while avoiding the severe minimality violations of the translation-based baseline. Compared to supervised fine-tuning, Macro achieves superior performance on both metrics, confirming that explicit preference optimization is essential for balancing this trade-off. Further analyses reveal that Macro increases cross-lingual perturbation alignment and mitigates common generation errors. Our results highlight preference optimization as a promising direction for enhancing multilingual model explanations.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Why Are LLM Backdoor Defenses Fragmented? A Feature-Level Explanation with Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a serious threat to large language models (LLMs), but existing defenses remain fragmented, failing to provide unified defense against both dirty-label and clean-label attacks. To investigate why such fragmentation arises, we present the first systematic feature-level mechanistic analysis of LLM backdoors using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Starting from a 2\times2 comparison of clean and poisoned models on clean and triggered inputs, we trace backdoor-induced logit shifts to high-contributing SAE features and categorize them into four roles: \textit{interaction}, \textit{suppressed}, \textit{mixed}, and \textit{weight-modified features}. This taxonomy reveals systematic encoding differences: dirty-label backdoors are dominated by isolated interaction features, whereas clean-label backdoors rely more on heterogeneous mixtures of mixed and weight-modified features. These differences explain why existing defenses remain fragmented across attack paradigms. We validate this hypothesis through inference-time feature clamping, which reduces ASR to at most **10.8%** in most dirty-label settings and at most **15.4%** in the majority of clean-label settings, while preserving benign-task performance. These results show that SAE-based analysis can explain defense fragmentation and guide interpretable backdoor mitigation.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Long-Short Memory Steering to Mitigate Unfaithful Self-Brainwashing
abstract: Although recent large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance, their reasoning processes remain vulnerable to external manipulation. We observe that LRMs can gradually rationalize incorrect user-provided hints during multi-step reasoning. Instead of rejecting false hints, models adapt their intermediate states to accommodate them and eventually produce seemingly coherent yet incorrect conclusions. We refer to this phenomenon as self-brainwashing and analyze it through empirical and theoretical analyses. We find that unfaithful reasoning steps are often locally detectable when models only focus on local reasoning context. However, this ability degrades over long reasoning trajectories, allowing unfaithful steps to accumulate and bias the final answer toward the hint. Motivated by these findings, we propose Long-Short Memory Steering (LSMS), a training-free inference-time framework that uses short-term reasoning hidden states to enhance faithfulness and long-term reasoning hidden states to maintain consistency. Across three open-source reasoning models and four reasoning datasets, LSMS consistently reduces unfaithful answer shifts while preserving benign accuracy. On average, it lowers the shifted ratio by more than 20 percentage points under three real-world hint-based threats.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Disagreeing Rationales: Rethinking Classification and Explainability Evaluation in Hate Speech Detection
abstract: Human disagreement is ubiquitous and well-known in labeling. However, variation in explanations, captured through token-level human rationales, remains far less explored. At the same time, it is unclear how to best evaluate human labels and rationales, or how to best aggregate rationales beyond majority vote, in light of this variation. Yet rationales can reveal the richness of human reasoning, which may differ in style, values, and interpretations, especially in subjective NLP tasks such as hate-speech detection. In this work, we unify diverse models, training strategies, loss functions, and existing evaluation metrics under a single protocol by systematically re-implementing them across different label and rationale representation spaces. Classification metrics are organized around two key properties—predictive and distributional—while explainability metrics through three complementary dimensions: plausibility, faithfulness, and complexity. In this unified evaluation framework, we assess model behavior across classification and explainability metrics, as well as metric sensitivity to the choice of label (hard and soft) and rationale representation space (hard, intermediate and soft). Results show that intermediate and soft representations better capture variation in labels and rationales, with metrics revealing complementary facets of the same property. These findings highlight the need to align evaluation with task goals and rethink subjective NLP evaluation to better reflect diverse human judgments.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: FaithRL: Learning to Reason Faithfully through Step-Level Faithfulness Maximization
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has markedly improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning. However, most RLVR pipelines rely on sparse outcome-based rewards, providing little supervision over intermediate steps and thus encouraging over-confidence and spurious reasoning, which in turn increases hallucinations. To address this, we propose FaithRL, a general reinforcement learning framework that directly optimizes reasoning faithfulness. We formalize a faithfulness-maximization objective and theoretically show that optimizing it mitigates over-confidence. To instantiate this objective, we introduce a geometric reward design and a faithfulness-aware advantage modulation mechanism that assigns step-level credit by penalizing unfaithful steps while preserving valid partial derivations. Across diverse backbones and benchmarks, FaithRL consistently reduces hallucination rates while maintaining (and often improving) answer correctness. Further analysis confirms that FaithRL increases step-wise reasoning faithfulness and generalizes robustly.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: When and How Should an Agent Clarify? CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain
abstract: Instruction-tuned LLMs faced with under-specified queries often commit to a single interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing confidently wrong answers. In our experiments, prompting alone is insufficient: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover the missing information. Addressing this failure requires learning two coupled skills: when to ask rather than answer and how to ask a question that recovers the disambiguating information. Existing recipes either address only one of these skills or require a separately trained critic. We propose CIGAsk, an RL recipe that teaches both skills through two complementary reward signals within a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, providing per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed reward at the terminal token based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to ask. Across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a smaller backbone. It also transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Does Accuracy Equal Evidence? Reasoning Faithfulness under KV Cache Compression
abstract: KV cache compression is commonly evaluated by final-answer accuracy, implicitly assuming that preserving the answer also preserves the reasoning that supports it. We test this assumption for large reasoning models and show that it can fail: under compression, answer-level cues and evidential support can remain differentially recoverable. We study this failure with a controlled fixed-trace replay protocol, which holds reasoning content fixed and isolates whether compression preserves usable information from an already available trace. We evaluate ten token-eviction KV compression methods and one quantization method on three models across mathematical reasoning, scientific QA, clinical calculation, and long-context retrieval. We measure final accuracy, answer-chain consistency, and perturbation faithfulness. Across tasks, token-eviction methods can preserve competitive final-answer accuracy while substantially degrading chain support or perturbation faithfulness. We call this the answer-evidence gap. A coverage-preserving quantization control is substantially less affected, suggesting that the failure is tied less to KV memory reduction itself than to losing access to parts of the reasoning trace.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Explication of Refusal: Jailbreaking LLMs by Exploiting Refusal Explanations
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) face a dilemma between helpfulness and harmlessness, where LLMs are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful by explaining their decisions. In this work, we observe a phenomenon caused by this dilemma. When asked to explain a refusal triggered by a harmful query, LLMs disclose exploitable elements in their refusal explanations. These elements allow attackers to induce the generation of harmful content. We formalize this vulnerability as Induced Refusal Explication (IRE). To identify and exploit IRE, we propose Explication of Refusal (EoR), a black-box and multi-turn jailbreak method with a dual-agent framework. EoR induces and analyzes refusal explanations from victim models and then generates follow-up queries to jailbreak them. We evaluate EoR across nine victim models. EoR achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of **37.05** within five turns. When we apply EoR to the queries that PAIR fails to jailbreak, EoR reaches an average ASR of **66.0** across the nine victim models, which demonstrates that exploiting refusal explanations is complementary to existing automated jailbreak methods. We release our data and code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EoR-6234.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SagE-QG: Skill-Aligned and Evidence-Grounded Educational Question Generation via Counterfactual Evidence Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Automatic Question Generation (QG) can make reading-comprehension practice and assessment scalable. For educational use, generated questions should diagnose a target comprehension skill and rely on the passage evidence an expert would use to write the question. Existing answer-aware and skill-conditioned QG methods improve controllability, but often leave these skill-to-question and evidence-to-question dependencies implicit. We present SagE-QG, a Skill-aligned and Evidence-Grounding Framework for Question Generation. SagE-QG exposes evidence-grounded trajectories, optimizes multi-aspect rewards for answerability, skill alignment, and human similarity, and applies Counterfactual Evidence Intervention in reinforcement learning. The intervention removes selected evidence and rewards the Interventional Grounding Gap between full-passage and masked-evidence generations. Experiments on three reading-comprehension QG datasets show that SagE-QG delivers stronger educational quality, especially in skill alignment and answerability, while achieving competitive reference-based results.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Faithful Autoformalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair
abstract: When an LLM formalizes natural language, how do we know the output is faithful? We propose a roundtrip verification approach which does not require ground-truth annotations: formalize a statement, translate the result back to natural language, re-formalize, and use a formal tool to check logical equivalence. When the two formalizations agree, this provides evidence of a faithful formalization. When they disagree, a stage-level diagnosis localizes the error to a specific translation step, and a scoped repair operator attempts to correct that step. We evaluate the framework on two statutory domains (the Texas Transportation Code and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Code) using two LLMs (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2) with three repair baselines. Diagnosis-guided scoped repair is the most effective method, with effectiveness contingent on the reliability of the diagnosis function. Across both domains and both models, under our full repair system, rules that fail the equivalence check show 1.4x-2.5x more NLI drift than rules that pass it.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Counterfactual Sensitivity Regularization for Trace-Sensitive Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models can produce correct final answers with reasoning traces that are incomplete, inconsistent, or weakly coupled to the answer. We study whether training can increase this coupling in structured reasoning domains. We introduce Counterfactual Sensitivity Regularization (CSR), a training objective that creates verifier-approved counterfactual edits to reasoning traces, such as changing an arithmetic operator or a logical relation, and penalizes models when the answer distribution remains unchanged after an edit that should change the computation. We evaluate this behavior with Counterfactual Outcome Sensitivity (COS), the fraction of originally correct examples on which a validity-breaking trace edit changes the final answer. Because COS is aligned with the CSR objective by construction, we report it jointly with counterfactual target accuracy, target coverage, and null-edit preservation, and alongside evidence collected outside the training loop: natural-unfaithfulness audits, external formal verification, input contrast sets, and trace-dependence probes. Across arithmetic, formal logic, multi-hop question answering, and biomedical QA, CSR substantially improves edit sensitivity while incurring small accuracy trade-offs. The gains are largest in domains where the edited operators can be identified and verified reliably; performance degrades as verifier precision falls. These results support CSR as a practical regularizer for trace-sensitive reasoning, not as a complete solution to explanation faithfulness.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Grounded Decoding: Retrieval-Anchored Probability Fusion for Faithful RAG
abstract: As retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems scale, ensuring faithful grounding in external evidence remains challenging. Large language models may still rely on parametric knowledge when it conflicts with retrieved information. We propose Grounded Decoding, a training-free decoding framework that improves factual consistency in RAG without modifying model parameters. At each generation step, our method constructs two matched-prompt distributions: a full RAG distribution conditioned on the query, retrieved documents, and generated prefix, and a retrieval-only distribution conditioned solely on the retrieved evidence and the same prefix. We derive the final next-token distribution as the unique solution to a KL-barycenter objective over the probability simplex, resulting in a normalized geometric fusion of the two distributions. The formulation recovers standard RAG when the grounding weight is zero and progressively shifts probability mass toward retrieved evidence as grounding strength increases. We further introduce a conflict-aware adaptive weighting scheme that adjusts grounding strength based on distributional disagreement and retriever confidence. Experiments on ALCE, Natural Questions, and FActScore show consistent improvements in factual accuracy and citation quality over standard RAG and competitive decoding-time baselines while maintaining fluency. These results suggest that probability-level fusion offers an effective and efficient alternative to logit-level intervention for faithful RAG decoding.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoLT-Drive: Counterfactual Long-Tail Benchmarking and Knowledge-Preserving Adaptation for Driving Affordance Prediction
abstract: Long-tail autonomous driving failures are often framed as rare-object recognition errors. We argue that this view is incomplete: the decision-critical question is not only whether a model recognizes an unusual object, but whether it infers how that object changes the ego vehicle’s feasible high-level actions. We formalize this problem as decision-level driving affordance prediction, where a model maps a front-view image, ego-motion history, and navigation command to a structured longitudinal–lateral meta-action. To evaluate this capability, we introduce CoLT-Drive, a 3,536-sample counterfactual long-tail benchmark that inserts rare objects into otherwise fixed driving scenes and measures whether models predict acceptable action pairs. To improve deployable small VLMs, we propose KPA, a knowledge-preserving adaptation framework that combines structured perception-to-decision prompting, SLERP-based expert merging, and RegMoE, a regime-aware LoRA mixture-of-experts module. KPA preserves the pretrained model’s open-world knowledge while allocating lightweight adaptation capacity to different driving decision regimes. Experiments on an in-domain driving split and CoLT-Drive show that KPA achieves 60.8% pair accuracy on CoLT-Drive, outperforming the pretrained Qwen3-VL-2B baseline (50.3%) and LoRA SFT (32.4%) while maintaining competitive in-domain accuracy.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Addressing the Concept Faithfulness Gap through Probe-Guided Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse, interpretable features, but these features often struggle to predict task-relevant concepts that remain clearly encoded in the original dense activations. We call this mismatch a concept faithfulness gap: a faithful SAE should preserve concept-level representations, such as toxicity or sentiment, rather than producing features that look interpretable but lose predictive relevance. We introduce ProbeSAE, a probing-guided fine-tuning framework that addresses this gap by preserving task-relevant concept structure in a more monosemantic sparse decomposition, enabling more effective causal control over model behaviour without sacrificing interpretability. We evaluate ProbeSAE on two SAE architectures (TopK, JumpReLU), two domains (toxicity, sentiment), and multilingual out-of-distribution settings spanning six languages. Trained exclusively on English data, ProbeSAE: (i) produces more predictive, monosemantic, and interpretable sparse features than pre-trained or naïvely fine-tuned SAEs across all six evaluation languages; (ii) learns language-independent feature directions, as confirmed by cross-lingual causal ablation; (iii) passes SAEBench evaluation, confirming these gains do not arise from task/domain overfitting. Together, these results show that the concept faithfulness gap in SAEs can be addressed through probe-guided training, improving monosemanticity and causal effectiveness without sacrificing interpretability, making probe-guided SAEs a more reliable tool for domain-specific interpretability analysis.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: The Illusion of \textit{What If}: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present \textbf{WhatIfBench}, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose \textbf{PRISM}, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Title It Right: Faithful and Attractive Paper Title Generation via Pareto Dominance Alignment
abstract: Generating academic paper titles requires balancing two key goals: faithfulness to the content and attractiveness to readers. Existing methods often treat title generation as a simple summarization task, producing accurate but unengaging titles. While multi-objective Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) offers a potential solution, our empirical analysis shows that combining conflicting objectives into a single reward is associated with substantial gradient interference during training. To address this problem, drawing inspiration from Pareto dominance in multi-objective optimization, we propose Multi-Objective Dominance Alignment (MODA), a data-centric training strategy tailored for academic title generation. MODA retains preference pairs with strict Pareto dominance, thereby reducing exposure to supervision with opposing reward directions. We implement MODA using dual reward models to independently score both dimensions. Across our experiments, this filtering strategy improves the observed balance between faithfulness and attractiveness, outperforms Human Author baselines, and approaches the performance of frontier models despite using an 8B backbone. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/realyoume/title_it_right.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SCHEDBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Constraint Faithfulness in Natural-Language Combinatorial Scheduling
abstract: This paper introduces **SCHEDBench**, a natural-language benchmark for evaluating **combinatorial scheduling** constraint faithfulness under surface-form variation. Grounded in canonical scheduling instances and solver-derived feasibility and optimality, SCHEDBench assesses whether large language models (**LLMs**) generate schedules with the same constraint-feasible behavior across varied natural-language (NL) surface forms. SCHEDBench spans 1,132 instances across job-shop scheduling problems (JSP), single and multi-mode resource-constrained project scheduling problems (RCPSP), nurse rostering/scheduling, and curriculum timetabling problems of varying difficulty. Instances are templated into natural language problems using domain-specific templates, themed entities, lexical-syntactic template rephrasing, and constraint-level surface-form variation—with reference solutions verified for feasibility and objective optimality. Across thirteen frontier and open-weight LLMs, we find that models are not reliably invariant to semantically equivalent renderings of the same scheduling problem. Surface-form variation reduces feasibility and induces above-noise shifts in per-instance hard-constraint violations on matched instances. Among the tested isolated axes, constraint reordering yields the clearest above-noise sensitivity.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: TimeClaimBench: A Claim-Level Benchmark for Grounded LLM Explanations of Time Series
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to explain numerical time series, but fluent explanations can misstate when a change occurs, overstate a trend, or introduce unsupported patterns. Existing evaluations often score forecasts, answers, or whole explanations, leaving claim-level temporal grounding undermeasured. We introduce TimeClaimBench, a benchmark that parses explanations into atomic temporal claims and verifies them against a deterministic extracted event graph. Across five LLMs on controlled synthetic series, event-grounded prompting raises the strict graph-supported rate by 18.3 points and reduces graph-unsupported claims by 27.9 points under this fixed operational criterion. Calibration analyses show the boundary of that result. The extractor recovers the designed primary event in 394 of 400 series, but this does not estimate the precision of additional extracted events. A blinded two-annotator comparison on one model and 40 series reverses the automatic ordering: holistic ratings favor Direct and chain-of-thought outputs over event-grounded outputs. therefore distinguishes four axes that should not be conflated: designed-event recovery, the unresolved precision of additional events, claim-to-graph consistency, and whole-explanation human judgment. Code: https://github.com/lunaaa95/TimeClaimBench
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CounterMem: Counterfactual Evaluation of Non-Parametric Memory Use in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is usually evaluated from one observed trace: the query, the retrieved context, and the generated answer. Such evaluations can tell us whether the answer is consistent with the retrieved context, but not whether the system would still give the same answer if that context were removed, updated, or contradicted. We introduce COUNTERMEM, an evaluation protocol for RAG systems that are expected to answer from retrieved evidence: it keeps the RAG configuration fixed, changes only the retrieved context, regenerates the answer, and records whether the answer changes in the expected direction. Across RAGBench, ExpertQA, and DelucionQA, COUNTERMEM complements observed-trace faithfulness by exposing failures it is not designed to see. Configurations that look equivalent under RAGAS faithfulness behave very differently once their evidence is removed, updated, or contradicted, and among RAGChecker-approved answers more than half silently miss coherent contradictions and over a third ignore coherent updates. The failures persist across generator and judge families, the behavioral detectors agree with blind human annotators as closely as the annotators agree with each other, and row-level intervention traces localize failures to retrieval, reranking, or generation. Artifact (protocol, prompts, detectors, scripts, audit traces): https://github.com/DeltaLabTLV/CounterMem.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ICE: Intervention-Consistent Explanation Evaluation with Statistical Grounding for LLMs
abstract: Evaluating whether explanations faithfully reflect a model’s reasoning remains an open problem. Existing benchmarks use single interventions without statistical testing, making it impossible to distinguish genuine faithfulness from chance-level performance. We show that faithfulness is not a fixed property but an operator-dependent quantity that changes with the intervention method used to measure it. We introduce ICE (Intervention-Consistent Explanation), a framework that evaluates explanations against random baselines of equal size under multiple operators. Evaluating 7 LLMs across 4 tasks with deletion and retrieval infill operators, we find that switching operators crosses the positive-evidence threshold in 18% of configurations (5 of 28 attention comparisons), with gaps reaching 44 percentage points. Randomized baselines detect anti-faithfulness (explanations worse than random) in nearly one-third of English deletion configurations, invisible without random comparisons. These patterns persist across 6 non-English languages and 2 attribution methods. The methodology generalizes to step-level chain-of-thought evaluation, where preliminary results on 3 frontier models suggest that high accuracy does not imply faithful reasoning.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Why Prompt-Injection Detectors Fail on XPIA: A Latent-Space Explanation
abstract: Prompt-injection detectors often fail on **cross-prompt-injection attacks (XPIA)**, where the adversarial instruction is hidden inside a document, email, webpage, or tool output. This paper argues that the failure is not only a **distribution-shift problem**, but also a **representation-level problem**. Inside the hidden states of frozen detector backbones, user prompt-injection attacks (UPIA) and XPIA are encoded along **distinct, weakly aligned directions**. A detector whose readout is primarily aligned with the UPIA direction can therefore miss the XPIA signal, even though both signals are present in the same model’s representation. A **two-axis linear-discriminant probe** recovers this missing signal: UPIA attacks fire the UPIA axis in **99.9%** of caught cases, while XPIA attacks fire the XPIA axis in **97.3%** of caught cases. Axis ablations and activation-level steering suggest that these directions are not only predictive but may also be behaviorally relevant under controlled perturbations. The geometry persists across model families, training stages, scales, and external prompt-injection benchmarks, suggesting that **XPIA should be treated as a distinct threat axis rather than as a harder version of UPIA**.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EDIT: Evidence-Diagnosed Intervention Training for Rule-Faithful LLM Grading
abstract: Reliable rubric grading requires more than accurate score prediction. Each judgement must be grounded in the mark scheme and evidence from the student answer. Existing credit-assignment and intervention methods, primarily designed for self-contained reasoning tasks such as mathematics reasoning, struggle in this setting because they do not identify where grading reasoning goes wrong or how the model’s belief about the final mark changes during reasoning. We propose Evidence-Diagnosed Intervention Training (EDIT), a two-phase framework for training more rubric-faithful LLM graders. First, EDIT-SFT locates problematic reasoning steps using internal model signals: posterior belief over the final mark and input-grounding scores. It then revises only these local steps with help from a rubric checklist. Second, EDIT-RL calibrates the grader with belief-guided reward shaping, penalising large harmful belief drifts while still allowing helpful exploration. Experiments on two real-world, multi-subject grading benchmarks demonstrate that EDIT consistently outperforms strong supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain splits, with ablation studies confirming that internal-state diagnostics drive these gains. Under deterministic rubric-edit interventions, EDIT-SFT is the most rule-responsive of all evaluated systems, and EDIT-RL largely retains this responsiveness while improving accuracy.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Faithfulness Evaluation for Decoder-Only LLM Attributions with Controlled Retained Information
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated with input attribution methods, yet comparing such explanations remains challenging. Existing soft-perturbation faithfulness metrics, such as Soft-NC and Soft-NS, can conflate attribution quality with the number of words retained during perturbation: attribution methods with larger average scores may keep more words and therefore obtain inflated scores. To address this issue, we propose \pi-Soft-NC and \pi-Soft-NS, an evaluation framework that compares attribution methods under the same expected retaining probability, thus controlling the number of retained words. We further introduce Grad-ELLM, a gradient-based attribution method tailored to autoregressive decoder-only LLMs, which combines gradient-derived channel importance with attention-derived token importance at each decoding step. Experiments on classification and open-generation tasks with Llama and Mistral show that Grad-ELLM achieves strong comprehensiveness-oriented faithfulness under \pi-Soft-NC, while there is no dominant method under \pi-Soft-NS. Our evaluation metric serves as a controlled evaluation framework to compare XAI methods for LLMs, which will support progress in the field.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ARMOR-PRM: Adversarially Robust Process Reward Models via Counterfactual Margins and Invariance Regularization
abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are vulnerable to reward hacking: policies exploit surface cues such as confident phrasing or structured formatting in place of logical correctness, which yields an inverted-U collapse under optimization pressure. We propose ARMOR-PRM, which augments standard PRM training with three regularizers: a counterfactual margin loss, an adversarial invariance loss with low-score anchoring, and a gradient penalty on the reward head. On ProcessBench (three splits; "math" excluded due to training data overlap), ARMOR-PRM improves Detection Rate by 14.9 percentage points and AUROC by 4.1 percentage points over Vanilla PRM, and is the only variant whose Best-of-N reranking accuracy improves monotonically through N=128. A domain-shift diagnostic further shows that objective-level robustness and data coverage are distinct but complementary axes: ARMOR-PRM responds best to iterative hard-negative retraining, suggesting a practical two-stage deployment path.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CoBRA: Learning Tool-Use Boundaries via Counterfactual Margins
abstract: As large language models increasingly act through external tools, deciding when to call a tool has become a central problem alongside deciding how to use it. Unnecessary tool calls introduce latency, cost, retrieval noise, and error propagation, while missed calls hurt knowledge-intensive queries or questions requiring up-to-date evidence. Existing methods typically trigger tools from absolute query or generation signals, such as difficulty, confidence, or final task reward, and therefore lack an explicit estimate of the instance-level marginal benefit of tool use. We propose CoBRA, a counterfactual boundary-learning framework for tool-augmented language models. CoBRA first constructs internal and external experts from the same base model, collects paired trajectories, and estimates the reward margin between answering with and without tools. This margin partitions data into internal-favored, external-favored, and ambiguous cases. CoBRA then uses clear-margin samples for Boundary-Aware Cold-Start SFT, followed by MARS-RL with reference-split rollouts and counterfactual marginal advantages to optimize boundary decisions. Experiments with retrieval as the main tool on Qwen3-4B show that CoBRA improves tool-use efficiency and boundary-sensitive answer accuracy while maintaining strong performance on tool-dependent out-of-distribution questions.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Do VLMs Read or Rewrite? On Transcription Faithfulness in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used in place of traditional OCR pipelines for document understanding. We show that VLMs do not always transcribe text literally. When the input contains imperfect text, they often rewrite it into a more plausible form, a behavior that clean-text OCR benchmarks do not detect. We introduce FaithC4, a multilingual perturbation benchmark of 1,455 single-page documents (English, Chinese, Korean) with three perturbation families: scramble, random substitution, and visually similar substitution. We use it to evaluate 15 systems spanning general-purpose VLMs, OCR-specialized VLMs, and traditional OCR pipelines. Traditional OCR is near-perfect on perturbed text, OCR-specialized VLMs degrade by 0.2–2.3 points of Word Error Rate (WER), and general-purpose VLMs degrade by up to 4.5 points in English language. To explain this gap, we probe Qwen3-VL-4B layer-by-layer and find that rewriting occurs when a perturbed word’s final-layer FFN representation stays close to the original word’s encoding, while faithful transcription occurs when the representation is sufficiently disrupted. Shorter words give the model less evidence to disrupt the representation and are therefore rewritten far more often than longer ones, with 4-character words rewritten more than ten times as often as words of 8 or more characters. We will release FaithC4 and our evaluation code upon acceptance to support future research on transcription faithfulness.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ReCite: Agentic Reasoning for Faithful Citation
abstract: Accurate citations are the foundation of academic writing, tracing intellectual origins and substantiating core claims. However, manually navigating the growing volume of scientific literature is increasingly difficult, prompting reliance on automatic citation recommendation. While modern retrieval-augmented architectures have largely mitigated the fabrication of non-existent papers, current systems relying on semantic similarity struggle with misattribution, often citing authentic papers that fail to logically support the author’s claim. To address this challenge, we argue that accurate citation requires a shift from similarity-based search to active, claim-level reasoning. We propose ReCite, a decoupled agentic framework that orchestrates location perception, intent-aware query planning, and reflective verification. Trained on synthesized reasoning trajectories, our agent verifies claim-evidence consistency and triggers self-correction loops when retrieved candidates lack logical support. Experiments demonstrate that our lightweight framework outperforms state-of-the-art massive generative models in strict citation accuracy. By grounding literature matching in verifiable logic rather than semantic overlap, ReCite establishes a reliable foundation for automated academic writing.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Counterfactual Self-Distillation: A Distribution-Shaping Framework for Entity-Fact Unlearning in Large Language Models
abstract: Entity-fact unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove the binding between a target entity and a forgotten fact, producing a model that behaves like one retrained without the forgotten data while preserving neighboring knowledge and overall model utility. We frame this problem as distribution shaping: such a retrained model would yield a plausible distribution at forget queries, fluent, semantically appropriate, and reflective of residual knowledge, which we take as the appropriate target. Existing objectives provide only narrow token-level or semantically uninformative supervision, falling short of this target. We propose Counterfactual Self-Distillation (CSD), a self-distillation framework that approximates the retrained distribution by constructing a counterfactual teacher through type-consistent entity substitution. The resulting teacher is decoupled from the target identity while preserving type-level relational structure, enabling directed probability reallocation without an external oracle. Experiments on TOFU and RWKU show that CSD achieves a strong forget-utility trade-off, including the best overall forgetting on RWKU and strong performance on TOFU.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Counterfactual Selective Imitation for Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Long-horizon agents with structured actions execute tasks through sequences of dependent decisions, so a local decision mistake can change later observations and cause the task to fail. Stronger expert models offer a natural source of supervision, yet direct imitation or behavior cloning treats many differences between expert and base actions as equally useful targets. In this paper, we propose counterfactual selective imitation (CSI), a method that uses same-state counterfactual comparison to identify positive return differences. CSI assigns expert targets only when counterfactual rollouts show a high positive return difference, and routine states receive base-policy targets. The learned update is restricted to structured action spans, leaves the base model frozen, and does not require expert queries or replay at deployment. Experiments on AppWorld, ToolSandbox, and WebShop show that CSI raises average task success from 33.3% to 49.7% over the Qwen3-8B base and reduces average invalid/tool error from 9.3% to 4.9%. Compared with the strongest same-deployment adaptation baseline, CSI improves average task success by 1.3 points with only 5% additional deployed-inference latency.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: SocialReasonBench: A Video-QA Benchmark for Social Reasoning with Counterfactual Narrative Videos
abstract: Recent advances in Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have greatly improved video understanding, yet their ability to reason about human-centered social situations remains limited. Existing benchmarks typically rely on videos with a single observed trajectory, making it difficult to determine whether models truly understand social dynamics or merely exploit recurring narrative patterns. We introduce SocialReasonBench, a video multiple-choice QA benchmark for evaluating socially grounded reasoning in scenarios derived from interactive narratives. Built from gameplay videos of Detroit: Become Human, the benchmark leverages branching storylines where player decisions lead to alternative social outcomes that can be checked against the game’s own script, flowchart, and recorded branches. We develop a multi-agent curation pipeline that localizes socially meaningful clips, grounds answer labels in game-state signals, and generates theory-guided questions with diagnostic distractors. SocialReasonBench covers seven reasoning dimensions, including intent recognition, emotional empathy, moral dilemma, counterfactual reasoning, and causal antecedent. Experiments on contemporary LMMs show that models perform reasonably well on basic social understanding but struggle with counterfactual and causal reasoning. Further ablation and diagnostic error analyses reveal that models often depend on incomplete modality cues and fall into reasoning traps such as visual shortcuts, highlighting a gap between observable event recognition and deeper reasoning over latent social states.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: RADAM: A Retrieval-Augmented Detection and Mitigation Framework for Faithfulness Hallucinations
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) empowers large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge but remains vulnerable to faithfulness hallucinations—answers that contradict retrieved evidence. We introduce RADAM, a lightweight post-processing framework that mitigates this issue via fine-grained hallucination detection and guided revision. RADAM leverages a single diagnostic critic, optimized via preference tuning on taxonomy-guided data, to generate structured critiques encompassing both precise error spans and explicit revision suggestions, which guide the base model toward more faithful outputs. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that RADAM consistently achieves the lowest average hallucination rate across the evaluated methods, while largely preserving response quality and achieving out-of-domain performance comparable to enterprise-grade LLMs.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: EviGen: Predictive Evidence Scaffolding for Verifiable Clinical Rationale Generation
abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) capture years of patient history across notes, codes, labs, and procedures, and contain evidence needed to reason about likely clinical outcomes. However, comprehensive clinician review of these records is impractical, and LLM-based processing is costly and often unreliable, missing some relevant observations while hallucinating others. We therefore propose **EviGen**, a three-layer framework for verifiable clinical rationale generation that addresses these challenges. The **first layer** is a patient-conditioned retriever that uses learnable queries to find evidence predictive of, not just textually relevant to, a clinical outcome and ranks it by prediction attribution scores. The **second layer** is an LLM generator that consumes this ranked evidence as a scaffold to produce a clinical rationale grounded in the retrieved spans. The **third layer** is a process-supervised verifier that checks the generated rationale at the reasoning-step level, flagging unreliable claims. Across three medical prediction datasets, EviGen improves prediction performance and rationale faithfulness over full-context LLM and RAG baselines, and is preferred by clinical reviewers in a usability evaluation.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Gaming the Judge: How Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought Can Undermine Agent Evaluation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to evaluate agent performance, particularly in non-verifiable settings where judgments rely on agent trajectories including chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. This paradigm implicitly assumes that the agent’s CoT faithfully reflects both its internal reasoning and the underlying environment state. We show this assumption is brittle: LLM judges are highly susceptible to manipulation of agent reasoning traces. By systematically rewriting agent CoTs while holding actions and observations fixed, we demonstrate that manipulated reasoning alone can increase false positive rates of state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM) judges by up to 117% relative to the unmanipulated baseline across 800 trajectories spanning diverse web tasks. We study manipulation strategies spanning style-based approaches that alter only the presentation of reasoning and content-based approaches that fabricate signals of task progress, and find that content-based manipulations are consistently more effective. We evaluate mitigation strategies including manipulation-aware prompting and judge-time scaling, which can reduce but do not eliminate the vulnerability. Our findings reveal a fundamental vulnerability in LLM-based evaluation and highlight the need for judging mechanisms that verify reasoning claims against observable evidence.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Agent4ExpRec: Towards Generating and Evaluating User-Centric Recommendation Explanation
abstract: Explainable Recommendation (ER) aims to improve the transparency of Recommender Systems (RS) by generating natural language explanations. However, existing methods primarily optimize textual similarity to reference explanations, which often leads to item-centric explanations focusing on product attributes rather than users’ personalized preferences. Moreover, they usually do not care how the generated explanations influence the behavior of users. To address these limitations, we introduce Agent4ExpRec, a closed-loop user-centric pipeline designed for generating and evaluating recommendation explanation. Based on the original explanations, it enables the peer agent to analyze the user’s requirements from multiple aspects and provides feedback, and automatically plans the refinement process to generate explanations focusing on user preferences. During the evaluation stage, we analyze how different explanations influence user behavior, providing evidence that our generated explanations are more consistent with users’ personalized preferences. Since the actual user behavior on large-scale explanation text is difficult to obtain in practice, we use LLM-powered agents equipped with user profile to simulate user interactions and decision-making in ER scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the generated explanations consistently align with user preferences, highlighting the potential of user-centric refinement for explainable recommendation tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/yy-Hou/Agent4ExpRec.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Rationale-Grounded In-Context Learning for Time Series Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: The underperformance of existing multimodal large language models for time series reasoning lies in the absence of rationale priors that connect temporal observations to their downstream outcomes, which leads models to rely on superficial pattern matching rather than principled reasoning. We therefore propose the rationale-grounded in-context learning for time series reasoning, where rationales work as guiding reasoning units rather than post-hoc explanations, and develop the RationaleTS method. Specifically, we firstly induce label-conditioned rationales, composed of reasoning paths from observable evidence to the potential outcomes. Then, we design the hybrid retrieval by balancing temporal patterns and semantic contexts to retrieve correlated rationale priors for the final in-context inference on new samples. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed RationaleTS on three-domain time series reasoning tasks. We provide the source code in https://github.com/yuppielqx/RationaleTS.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Towards Faithful and Controllable Personalization via Critique-Post-Edit Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning has driven the largest post-training gains on tasks with verifiable rewards, such as code and math. Extending this success to subjective tasks remains difficult: good responses must satisfy multiple soft criteria simultaneously, and no scalar reward can indicate which aspect of a response should improve. Personalization is a clear instance of this. A personalized response must balance helpfulness, user-specific relevance, and naturalness, yet standard verifiers cannot localize which specific dimension needs improvement. In this regime, supervised fine-tuning quickly saturates, and PPO with Bradley-Terry reward models is prone to reward hacking, especially via length bias, producing verbose or superficially personalized responses. We propose Critique-Post-Edit, an RL framework that combines (1) a personalized Generative Reward Model (GRM) producing multi-dimensional scores and natural-language critiques, and (2) a critique-guided editing step that turns feedback into nearby alternative responses for policy learning. The reward signal stays scalar; our contribution is to use personalized critiques to construct more informative local alternatives (responses close to the on-policy rollout in edit distance) during training. Under length-controlled evaluation, Critique-Post-Edit improves over PPO by 11.0 and 11.6 win-rate points on Qwen2.5-7B and 14B models, respectively. Notably, the 14B model matches or outperforms GPT-4.1 on the evaluated benchmarks. A static mechanism study further shows that critique-guided edits stay more local than extra rollouts and shift scores more favorably than generic rewrites. All of our experiments are on personalization; systematic evaluation on other subjective tasks is left to future work.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Case-based Statute Retrieval for Multi-turn Legal Consultation with Fact-level and Rationale-level Mixed Evidence Graphs
abstract: Statute retrieval in multi-turn legal consultation is challenging because users often describe evolving facts in colloquial language, while statutes formulate legal conditions in abstract terms. This mismatch makes direct query–statute matching insufficient to capture the intermediate evidence needed to determine statutory applicability. Legal cases can bridge this gap by documenting how concrete facts and legal rationales support applicable statutes. However, case retrieval is noisy: factually similar cases may concern different legal issues, whereas cases with dissimilar surface facts may share the same applicability rationale. We propose FR-MEG, a Fact-level and Rationale-level Mixed Evidence Graph for turn-level statute retrieval. FR-MEG organizes case-derived evidence into two complementary views that model case–statute relationships through factual descriptions and legal rationales. The two views are calibrated and fused with full-corpus LegalDense retrieval, enabling case evidence to improve statute ranking without limiting candidates to graph-covered statutes. Experiments on LexRAG show that FR-MEG improves Recall@10 from 38.83% to 43.81% and NDCG@10 from 25.64% to 28.23% over the LegalDense backbone.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CPSD: Counterfactual Patches Self-Distillation in RLVR
abstract: Self-distillation in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses successful in-group rollouts to teach the failed ones, with no external teacher needed. Whether it actually helps turns on three closely related design questions that the canonical method does not handle carefully: how to construct an appropriate teacher context for a given loser, where in the response the distillation loss should act, and what kind of signal it should carry. The canonical Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) instantiation answers all three by default: a random in-group winner, a global distillation loss on the whole response, and a Jensen–Shannon divergence on the full top-K distribution. These three defaults compound into a catastrophic late-training failure that short-horizon evaluation hides. We propose CPSD (Counterfactual Patches Self-Distillation), which replaces each default in turn: pick the teacher by minimum embedding-weighted edit distance, localise distillation to an adaptive-stop counterfactual patch beginning at the first divergent token, and replace JS with a Plackett–Luce listwise loss that preserves only the teacher’s ranking. Across six reasoning benchmarks at a fixed 150-step budget, CPSD eliminates the SDPO cliff and lifts average accuracy by +5.7 pp over GRPO on Qwen3-8B and +4.2 pp on Qwen3-4B.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Beyond Fooling: Model Manipulation Under Explanation-aware Training
abstract: Feature-level explanations are commonly used to interpret transformer-based NLP models. Still, little is known about how explanation-aware objectives influence model behaviour during training. While prior work has demonstrated training-time manipulation of explanations in vision models, its implications for transformers and token-level explainability remain unexplored. We study training-time manipulation of token-level explanations in transformer-based NLP classifiers and introduce sequence-aware objectives suited to text input. We show that explanation-aware training systematically alters token relevance patterns while largely preserving task accuracy. Importantly, masking and cross-method evaluations reveal that these attribution changes can coincide with shifts in functional model reliance rather than isolated failures of specific explanation methods. Our results suggest that apparent vulnerabilities of feature-level explanations can reflect deeper model adaptations, underscoring the need to consider learning dynamics when interpreting explanation robustness.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: PragReST: Self-Reinforcing Counterfactual Reasoning for Pragmatic Language Understanding
abstract: Natural language understanding often depends on meanings that are implied rather than explicitly stated, requiring pragmatic reasoning. Despite strong performance on math and logical reasoning, large language models (LLMs) still trail humans on pragmatic inference, often defaulting to literal interpretations. To improve LLM pragmatic reasoning, we introduce PragReST, a self-supervised framework that constructs pragmatic QA data, generates counterfactual reasoning traces, and trains models to internalize them through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, without human-labeled training data or distillation from a stronger teacher. Across four pragmatic benchmarks (PRAGMEGA, LUDWIG, METOQA, and ALTPRAG) and multiple model families, including Qwen3, Gemma, and GPT-OSS, PragReST consistently improves over backbone models, task-specific pragmatic tuning baselines, and non-counterfactual variants of the same pipeline. On accuracy-based benchmarks, PragReST improves over the instruct backbone by 5.37% and 5.50% (absolute) for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, respectively. Our error analysis and ablations underscore the importance of counterfactual reasoning: PragReST primarily reduces errors caused by failures to contrast observed utterances with plausible alternatives, and removing counterfactual reasoning substantially reduces performance. Moreover, our training preserves out-of-domain performance on general-knowledge and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Balancing Faithfulness and Performance in Reasoning via Multi-Listener Soft Execution
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning sometimes fails to faithfully reflect the true computation of a large language model (LLM), hampering its utility in explaining how LLMs arrive at their answers. Moreover, optimizing for faithfulness and interpretability in reasoning often degrades task performance. To address this tradeoff and improve CoT faithfulness, we propose Reasoning Execution by Multiple Listeners (REMuL), a multi-party reinforcement learning approach. REMuL builds on the hypothesis that reasoning traces which other parties can follow will be more faithful. A speaker model generates a reasoning trace, which is truncated and passed to a pool of listener models who “execute” the trace, continuing the trace to an answer. Speakers are rewarded for producing reasoning that is clear to listeners, with additional correctness regularization via masked supervised finetuning to counter the tradeoff between faithfulness and performance. On multiple reasoning benchmarks (BIG-Bench Extra Hard, MuSR, ZebraLogicBench, and FOLIO), REMuL consistently and substantially improves three measures of faithfulness – hint attribution, early answering area over the curve (AOC), and mistake injection AOC – while also improving accuracy. Our analysis finds that these gains are robust across training domains and are associated with shorter and more direct CoTs.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CultureScore: Evaluating Cultural Faithfulness in Video Generation Models
abstract: As video generation models like Veo 3.1 and LTX-2 advance, their ability to accurately represent diverse global cultures remains a critical yet understudied frontier. Current metrics, such as VideoScore, only measure visual quality but offer no mechanism for assessing cultural faithfulness. Consequently, a model that replaces a Namaste with a handshake receives the same score as one that generates the gesture correctly. We propose CultureScore, a compositional evaluation framework that decomposes cultural faithfulness into three granular dimensions: Identity (who is represented), Context (culturally localized background), and Behavior (normative gestures and interactions). We operationalize this framework through an evaluation suite spanning 10 countries, yielding 6,174 generated videos across three state-of-the-art models. Our evaluation reveals that no current model achieves culturally faithful video generation: the best-performing model reaches only 56.8% overall CultureScore, with Behavior the most challenging dimension; no model exceeds 52.1% on behavior. Furthermore, the highest-scoring model (LTX-2) on visual quality was ranked last by native annotators, while CultureScore’s Behavior dimension shows the strongest positive correlation with human cultural judgment among the automatic metrics we evaluate, underscoring that cultural faithfulness is an essential criterion for equitable video generation. Data and code are publicly available.[<https://huggingface.co/datasets/ankurani/CultureScore>]
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Listwise Explanation of Embedding-Based Rankings via Semantic Chunk Grouping
abstract: Dense embedding rankers score documents through contextual sentence- and passage-level representations, yet listwise explanation methods often attribute rankings to isolated words. We study this mismatch and introduce ChunkGroupSHAP, a listwise Shapley method that clusters semantically related chunks across documents into shared features, preserving contextual evidence while bounding the KernelSHAP regression dimension by the group count. Across MS MARCO, FinanceBench, AILACaseDocs, and FinQA with E5-family rankers and BM25, raw chunks improve rank-reconstruction Fidelity over RankSHAP’s word features in all 11 dense-ranker settings. The best chunk-group configuration further improves on raw chunks in eight of these settings, with the incremental benefit depending on grouping scope; word features remain strongest in three of four BM25 settings. These results show that explanation units should match the ranking model: contextual chunks better suit dense bi-encoders, whereas words remain effective for BM25. ChunkGroupSHAP supports listwise attribution over contextual evidence through a bounded feature space shared across documents.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: CArtBench: A Museum-Grounded Benchmark for Evidence-Faithful Chinese Art Understanding
abstract: We introduce CARTBENCH, a museum-grounded benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on Chinese artworks beyond short-form recognition and QA. CARTBENCH comprises four subtasks: CURATORQA for evidence-grounded recognition and reasoning, CATALOGCAPTION for structured four-section expert-style appreciation, REINTERPRET for defensible reinterpretation with expert ratings, and CONNOISSEURPAIRS for original-copy discrimination under visually similar confounds. CARTBENCH is built by aligning image-bearing Palace Museum objects from Wikidata with authoritative catalog pages, spanning five art categories across multiple dynasties. Across evaluated VLMs, high overall CURATORQA accuracy can mask sharp drops on evidence-heavy and style-to-period questions; long-form appreciation remains far from expert references; and original-copy discrimination remains near chance. A held-out protocol-replication pilot on 120 artworks from five external institutions reproduces the main task-difficulty pattern, while not preserving the exact overall model ranking.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: ARTKGC: Leakage-Controlled Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion for Artwork Explanation
abstract: Explaining an artwork requires knowledge beyond visual recognition, including facts about its creator, subject, material, style, collection, and historical context. Knowledge graphs can provide such evidence, but artwork KGs are incomplete, especially for newly encountered artworks. We introduce ArtKGC, a leakage-controlled multimodal benchmark and evaluation protocol for artwork knowledge graph completion. ArtKGC links artworks to Wikidata facts, Wikipedia descriptions, and visual evidence while controlling ambiguous mappings, graph leakage, and descriptions that directly reveal held-out answers. We show that graph-only models are weak for unseen artworks, raw text can inflate evaluation through answer leakage, and visual evidence is strongly relation-dependent. As an interpretable diagnostic baseline, we use a validation-calibrated reranker that combines structural, sentence-redacted textual, and visual evidence. Experiments show improved completion in the primary inductive-artwork setting and modest downstream evidence gains for artwork QA and explanation diagnostics.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: MulEG: Multi-Level Explanation-Guided Feature Attribute Graph for Zero-Shot Tabular Classification
abstract: Zero-shot classification for structured tabular data has attracted increasing attention in recent years. An important line of research is leveraging textual explanations as supervision to improve the modeling of tabular attribute features. Previous studies usually serialize tabular data into flattened explanation sequences, or employ logical rules to model directional associations between tabular attributes and labels. However, these methods often suffer from two major limitations: the former disrupts the inherent row-column topological structure of tables, while the latter mainly represents relations with fixed logical operators or aggregation weights, making it difficult to model learnable dependencies among features. To address these issues, we propose a novel method (MulEG), which harnesses multi-level textual explanations with a feature attribute graph to model both tabular topology and cell-element relations. Specifically, to preserve the intrinsic row-column topological structure of tables, we propose a multi-level textual explanation modeling with sample-level, attribute-level, and label-level perspectives. Moreover, to capture fine-grained feature dependencies, we propose a differentiable message-passing mechanism using a feature attribute graph that allows heterogeneous features to propagate through message passing. Finally, extensive experimental results on datasets covering sixteen tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Counterfactual Tests for Measuring Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Visual Language Models
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) may often look plausible, yet it may not faithfully reflect the model’s decision-making process. While methods for measuring the faithfulness of CoTs for textual inputs have been increasingly introduced, using these methods for visual inputs is not straightforward. In this work, we adapt the family of counterfactual methods for measuring CoT faithfulness, namely the Counterfactual Test (CT) and Correlational Counterfactual Test (CCT), to visual inputs, and call them vCT and vCCT, respectively. Using vCT and vCCT, we benchmark eight recent open-source Vision Language Models (VLMs) on two datasets. Our analysis shows that CoTs do not reliably track visual evidence that influences model predictions: they may omit the removed object even when its removal causes a large prediction shift, yet mention it when the shift is small. We further find that Predict-then-Explain explanations align more strongly with perturbation-induced probability shifts than pre-answer CoTs, while binary vCT scores are often nearly saturated. We also include a reconstruction control, in which images pass through the same editing pipeline without object removal, and find that the main object-removal intervention induces larger shifts than reconstruction alone. We construct and release Counter-SNLI-VE and Counter-A-OKVQA, two datasets of image pairs that differ by a single object.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: LiveClawBench: Toward Faithful Evaluation of Stateful LLM Assistants
abstract: OpenClaw-style personal assistants extend LLM agents from isolated tool use to open-ended, stateful, and personalized software environments. Evaluating these assistants is fundamentally a fidelity problem: benchmarks must be faithful both to the distribution of real assistant tasks and to the execution semantics of the environments in which those tasks unfold. Existing benchmarks often lose fidelity in one dimension or the other. Their task distributions are shaped by what is easy to isolate, mock, and verify, underrepresenting real-world difficulties such as cross-service dependency, contaminated state, implicit intent, and runtime change. Their environments are either live but hard to reproduce, or reproducible but reduced to endpoint-level stubs that remove sessions, artifacts, state transitions, and downstream side effects. We introduce LiveClawBench, a benchmark designed around this dual-fidelity requirement. LiveClawBench combines a Triple-Axis Complexity Framework for difficulty-driven task construction with reproducible full-stack mock applications that preserve stateful execution semantics. With 134 executable cases across 10 domains with 22 mocked services, LiveClawBench supports controlled, extensible, and factor-level diagnostic evaluation of realistic agentic tasks.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Quantifying Retriever-Generator Alignment in RAG with Local Explanations
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems combine dense retrievers and language models to ground outputs in external documents. However, the interaction between these components remains opaque, creating challenges for deployment in high-stakes domains. We present RAG-E, an end-to-end explainability framework that quantifies retriever-generator alignment through mathematically grounded attribution methods. Our approach adapts Integrated Gradients for retriever analysis, proposes a Monte Carlo-stabilized Shapley Value approximation for generator attribution, and introduces the *Weighted Alignment between Retriever and Generator* (WARG) metric to measure how closely the generator’s document usage aligns with retriever rankings. Experiments on PopQA, QAMPARI, and TREC CAST datasets reveal substantial misalignment: depending on the model and setting, generators often ignore top-ranked documents and rely on documents ranked as less relevant. We show that WARG captures retriever-generator alignment better than Pearson and Spearman correlations and can serve as an indicator of RAG performance. RAG-E and WARG provide a practical framework for auditing this interaction, enabling more reliable and transparent RAG systems.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026

title: Trust the Uncertain Teacher: Distilling Dark Knowledge via Calibrated Uncertainty
abstract: The core of knowledge distillation lies in transferring the teacher’s rich ’dark knowledge’—subtle probabilistic patterns that reveal how classes are related and the distribution of uncertainties. While this idea is well established, teachers trained with conventional cross-entropy often fail to preserve such signals. Their distributions appear decisive but are in fact brittle, offering little beyond the hard label. This overconfidence is especially problematic in high-cardinality tasks, where subtle distinctions among many plausible classes are crucial for guiding compact students. To address this limitation, we revisit distillation from a distributional perspective and propose Calibrated Uncertainty Distillation (CUD), a framework that makes dark knowledge more faithfully accessible. Instead of uncritically inheriting the teacher’s overconfidence, CUD encourages the teacher to expose informative uncertainty and guides the student to learn from calibrated targets instead of overly sharpened predictions. By shaping the teacher’s predictive distribution before transfer, our approach balances accuracy and calibration, allowing students to benefit from both confident signals on easy cases and structured uncertainty on hard ones.
